tool.name: LandFacetMahalanobis

summary.para: One Mahalanobis distance cost (resistance) surface per land facet: how far every cell on the landscape departs, in multivariate standard deviations, from the conditions typical of that facet. The mean vector and covariance matrix come only from the facet's cells inside the Wildland Blocks, which act as training data, while the surface itself covers the whole analysis area. Each facet gets its own single-band raster, ready to use directly as the resistance surface in least-cost corridor modelling. If a Land Facet Density raster is supplied, density joins the analysis with a characteristic value of 100 percent rather than its mean, as the Land Facet method requires. Needs no Spatial Analyst. Part of the Land Facet Corridor Designer tool family.

tool.usage:
What this tool does. This is the third step of a Land Facet corridor analysis, after Land Facet Clustering and Land Facet Density. For each land facet in turn it works out what that facet typically looks like -- its average elevation, steepness, insolation, soil depth, or whatever variables you defined it with -- and then scores every cell in the study area by how far it departs from that description. The score is a Mahalanobis distance, which can be read as the number of multivariate standard deviations between a cell's conditions and the facet's prototype. Low scores mark ground that is most like the facet. Because a corridor should run through ground the target facet's species can actually use, that score is exactly what a least-cost model wants for resistance, so the output is used directly as the cost surface.
Why Mahalanobis rather than plain distance. Variables are measured in different units and are usually correlated: elevation in metres, steepness in degrees, density as a proportion. A plain (Euclidean) distance would let whichever variable happens to have the biggest numbers dominate, and would double-count two variables that carry the same information. Mahalanobis distance uses the covariance matrix to rescale every variable to comparable terms and to discount the redundancy between correlated ones, so each variable contributes on its merits. A constant Mahalanobis distance traces an ellipse (or a hyper-ellipsoid) around the prototype rather than a circle.
The Wildland Blocks restrict the sample, not the output. This is the point most easily misread, so it is worth being explicit about why the surface covers ground the blocks do not.
The Wildland Blocks are polygons understood to contain viable habitat that currently supports a community of species. That is what makes them useful: they are places where we already know the land works. We therefore use them as something close to training data. Within the blocks, the tool measures what each land facet actually looks like -- its characteristic elevation, steepness, insolation, soil depth, density, or whatever variables you defined it with -- and treats that description as the definition of good habitat for that facet.
Having learned that definition, the tool then applies it to the rest of the landscape. Every cell in the analysis area is scored by how closely it matches, so "best" throughout the output means "most like what exists inside the Wildland Blocks." The statistics are computed from a small, trusted sample; the scoring is done everywhere.
That everywhere is the whole point. The reason for the analysis is to connect the habitat blocks to each other, and a connection has to run across the land in between -- land that is, by definition, outside the blocks. To route that connection over the best available ground, we first have to know where good ground occurs outside the blocks, which means scoring the matrix, the gaps, and everything else a corridor might cross. A surface that stopped at the block boundaries would describe only the places that already need no connecting.
So expect the output to extend well beyond the Wildland Blocks, and expect much of the interesting variation to lie between them. That is correct and necessary, not a sign that the blocks were ignored.
Density's ideal is 100 percent, not its mean. Every variable normally contributes its sample mean to the prototype. The density variable is the exception. The prototypical cell of a land facet is one whose whole neighborhood is that same facet, so the characteristic value used is 1.0 (100 percent), even though the mean density actually observed is usually far lower. Beier and Brost are explicit that 100 percent is used "even if the 100 percent value is far above the mean." Only the mean is replaced; the covariance matrix still uses the real observed densities, so the spread and the correlations stay honest. In the original ArcMap workflow this was a manual edit the analyst had to remember to make after building the statistics tables; here it is applied automatically from the density raster's own metadata, and the tool reports the substitution in its run messages so you can see it happen.
What the density variable adds, and what you lose without it. The density raster is optional. With it, the cost surface prefers the interiors of facet patches -- places where the facet is genuinely abundant -- over isolated cells that merely happen to have the right elevation and slope. Without it, the surface still describes how closely each cell resembles the facet's typical conditions, but it has no notion of neighborhood context, so a lone matching cell in a sea of something else scores as well as the middle of a large patch. That is a legitimate analysis, but it is not the published method, and the tool warns when density is omitted.
One raster per facet, not one multi-band raster. The Land Facet Density tool writes a single multi-band raster because this toolbox consumes it itself. These cost surfaces are different: they are handed on to CorridorDesigner or the Cost Distance tools, which expect a single-band cost surface. So each facet gets its own raster, named from the output prefix and the facet's label, for example "Mahal_Valley_Cluster_2". Give the tool a folder or a geodatabase as the output workspace; a folder gets GeoTIFFs.
Progress. The meter advances one increment for each cost surface written, and the label names the facet being worked on -- "Facet 3 of 12: Ridge, Cluster 2" -- so you can see both what the tool is doing and how much is left. Within a facet the bar continues to creep as the surface is computed row by row. The two preparation steps, aligning the variable rasters and restricting the sample to the Wildland Blocks, run first and are labelled as such.
Variable order, and why it is filled in for you. The mean vector, the covariance matrix and the variable list must all be in the same order, and a mismatch produces distances that are wrong without looking wrong. When the land facet raster was made by the Land Facet Clustering tool it carries a record of exactly which rasters were used and in what order, and this tool fills the variable list in from that record, matching on the recorded catalog path first so a renamed layer still resolves. You can override the list, but do so knowing that the order is load bearing.
Pairing the density raster. Because the density raster holds one band per facet and band names do not survive being copied into a geodatabase, the mapping from band to facet lives in the raster's metadata. The tool checks that mapping against the land facet raster and responds in proportion to the risk. If both record the same analysis, it proceeds silently. If they record different analyses but the density raster still covers every facet present, it warns -- most likely the clustering was re-run. If the density raster has no band for some facet, or carries no record at all, the tool stops. That case is refused rather than warned about because the damage would be invisible: a wrong band means the surface is built from another facet's density, and since density's ideal is 100 percent that does not look like noise -- it systematically drags the corridor toward ground where the wrong facet is abundant, and the result looks entirely plausible.
Output values. Squared distance (D2) is the default and is the form traditionally used in ecological modelling; it rises steeply with departure from the prototype, which is usually the behaviour wanted from a resistance surface. Distance (D) is the square root of that and reads directly as "how many standard deviations from typical," which some find easier to interpret. The Chi-square p-value converts D2 to a probability and is the most intuitive of the three, but unlike the other two it assumes the variables are multivariate normal, so treat it as a presentation choice rather than a safer one.
When a facet is skipped. Each facet needs enough cells inside the Wildland Blocks to estimate a covariance matrix -- at minimum one more cell than there are variables, and in practice a great deal more. A facet that barely occurs inside the blocks, or one whose variables carry no variance there (for example a facet that forms a single solid patch, so its density is 1.0 at every sampled cell), produces a singular covariance matrix that cannot be inverted. The tool reports the condition number, names the facet, skips it, and carries on with the rest rather than abandoning the whole run. If this happens often, either the Wildland Blocks are too small to represent those facets or two of your variables are carrying the same information; the pseudo-inverse option under Advanced will force a result, but a singular matrix is usually telling you something real about the data.
Performance. The variable rasters are aligned to a common grid once, then each facet costs one statistics pass over the sample cells plus one pass over the whole grid to write its surface, so run time grows roughly in proportion to the number of facets. This tool honors no geoprocessing environments.
References. Land Facet Corridor Designer: Beier, P., and B. Brost. 2010, "Use of land facets to plan for climate change: conserving the arenas, not the actors," Conservation Biology 24:701-710 (https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1523-1739.2010.01422.x); Brost, B.M., and P. Beier. 2012, "Use of land facets to design linkages for climate change," Ecological Applications 22:87-103 (https://doi.org/10.1890/11-0213.1); Jenness, J., B. Brost, and P. Beier. 2013, "Land Facet Corridor Designer: Extension for ArcGIS," Jenness Enterprises (http://www.jennessent.com/arcgis/land_facets.htm). Corridor Designer tools: Majka, D., J. Jenness, and P. Beier. 2007, "CorridorDesigner: ArcGIS tools for designing and evaluating corridors" (http://corridordesign.org). Mahalanobis distance: Mahalanobis, P.C. 1936, "On the generalised distance in statistics," Proceedings of the National Institute of Sciences of India 2:49-55 (http://insa.nic.in/writereaddata/UpLoadedFiles/PINSA/Vol02_1936_1_Art05.pdf). Corridor resistance from Mahalanobis distance: Clevenger, A.P., J. Wierzchowski, B. Chruszcz, and K. Gunson. 2002, "GIS-generated, expert-based models for identifying wildlife habitat linkages and planning mitigation passages," Conservation Biology 16:503-514 (https://doi.org/10.1046/j.1523-1739.2002.00328.x).

dialogReference.para: The single-band land facet raster whose facets are to be modelled, normally the output of the Land Facet Clustering tool. When it carries that tool's linkage record, the variable list and the facet list below are filled in automatically from it, and every output is labelled with its category and cluster. Any other categorical raster works, but you will have to supply the variables yourself and the facets will be labelled by cell value.

The Wildland Blocks: polygons understood to contain viable habitat that currently supports a community of species. They act as training data. Each facet's mean vector and covariance matrix are computed only from that facet's cells falling inside these polygons, so what the tool learns is what the facet looks like where the land is known to work.

They do not limit the output. That definition of good habitat is then applied to the whole analysis area, because the aim is to connect the blocks to one another and a connection has to cross the ground in between -- ground that lies outside the blocks by definition. Finding where block-quality habitat occurs out there is precisely what the surface is for, so expect it to extend well past these polygons.
If features are selected, only the selection is used.

param.name: variables
param.displayname: Variable rasters (same order used for clustering)

dialogReference.para: The continuous variable rasters that define the facets -- typically the same ones used for the clustering. The order matters: the mean vector and covariance matrix are built in this order, and a mismatch produces distances that are wrong without looking wrong. When the land facet raster carries a linkage record this list is filled in from it automatically, matched on the recorded catalog path so a renamed layer still resolves. Elevation, insolation and steepness are the variables Beier and Brost recommend for topographic land facets, but any continuous topographic or soil variables may be used.

The multi-band output of the Land Facet Density tool, holding one band per facet. When supplied, density is added as a variable with a characteristic value of 100 percent rather than its mean, which makes the cost surface prefer the interiors of facet patches over isolated matching cells. Leave it empty to model the facets on their other variables alone. The tool reads the band-to-facet mapping from the raster's metadata and refuses a density raster that does not cover the facets in your land facet raster, because a mismatched band would silently pull the corridor toward the wrong ground.

Optionally restrict the run to particular land facets, one output raster each. Leave empty to build a cost surface for every facet, which is the normal choice. When the input carries a linkage record the list offers each facet by identifier and label. Restricting is useful for re-running a single facet, or for testing settings before committing to a long run.

Where the cost surfaces are written -- a folder or a geodatabase. One single-band raster is created per facet, not one multi-band raster, because these are handed on to least-cost corridor tools that expect a single-band cost surface. A folder destination produces GeoTIFFs.

The leading part of each output name; the facet's label is appended, giving names such as "Mahal_Valley_Cluster_2". Characters that a dataset name cannot contain are replaced with underscores, and a trailing underscore on the prefix is absorbed rather than doubled. Defaults to "Mahal_".

Squared distance (D2) is the default and the form traditionally used in ecological modelling; it rises steeply with departure from the prototype, which is normally what a resistance surface should do.
Distance (D) is its square root and reads directly as the number of multivariate standard deviations from typical.
The Chi-square p-value is the most intuitive to interpret but, unlike the other two, assumes the variables are multivariate normal.

How the covariance matrix is inverted. Standard is correct for well-behaved data and will stop with a clear message if the matrix is singular -- which usually means a variable has no variance among the sampled cells, or two variables are carrying the same information. The pseudo-inverse (SVD) will produce a result anyway; use it only when you understand why the matrix is singular and accept the consequence, since a singular matrix is often telling you something real about the data or the sample.

param.name: save_tables
param.displayname: Also save each facet's mean vector and covariance table

dialogReference.para: If checked, each facet's mean vector and covariance matrix are also written as tables beside its raster, named with the raster's name plus "_Mean" and "_Cov". They record the prototype the surface was built from -- including the substituted density ideal of 1.0 in the mean table -- which is useful for review, for reporting, and for reproducing a result later. In a folder they are written as dBASE tables.

scriptExample.title: Land Facet Mahalanobis example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: A cost surface for every facet using density, then a run without density, then a single facet with its statistics tables. Valid out_type values are exactly: "Squared distance (D2): Traditional for ecological modeling", "Distance (D)", "Chi-square p-value". Valid inversion values: "Standard (inverse)", "Pseudo-inverse (SVD)". Pass None for the density raster to leave it out. The variable order must match the order used to define the facets.
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
# One cost surface per facet, with density (the published method) arcpy.jenness.LandFacetMahalanobis( "landfacets.tif", "wildland_blocks", ["elevation.tif", "insolation.tif", "slope.tif"], "landfacets_Density.tif", None, r"C:\project\cost", "Cost", "Squared distance (D2): Traditional for ecological modeling", None, False)
# Without density: resemblance to the facet's typical values only arcpy.jenness.LandFacetMahalanobis( "landfacets.tif", "wildland_blocks", ["elevation.tif", "insolation.tif", "slope.tif"], None, None, r"C:\project\cost_nodens", "Cost", "Squared distance (D2): Traditional for ecological modeling", None, False)
# Just facets 3 and 7, saving each one's mean vector and covariance table arcpy.jenness.LandFacetMahalanobis( "landfacets.tif", "wildland_blocks", ["elevation.tif", "insolation.tif", "slope.tif"], "landfacets_Density.tif", "3;7", r"C:\project\cost", "Cost", "Distance (D)", "Standard (inverse)", True)

dataIdInfo.idCredit: Jeff Jenness, Brian Brost and Paul Beier, from the Land Facet Corridor Tools (corridordesign.org). A modernized port of the Land Facet Corridor Designer's Mahalanobis tools (Jenness, Brost and Beier 2013). Method after Mahalanobis (1936); Beier and Brost (2010), Conservation Biology 24:701-710; Brost and Beier (2012), Ecological Applications 22:87-103; corridor resistance after Clevenger, Wierzchowski, Chruszcz and Gunson (2002), Conservation Biology 16:503-514.
